stem: Which part of the plant is best suited for making virus-free plants and why?
solution:
The **meristem (apical and axillary)** is best suited for making virus-free plants.

**Reason:** even when the plant is infected with a virus, its meristem remains **free of virus**. The meristem can therefore be removed and grown **in vitro** (tissue culture) to recover healthy, virus-free plants. Meristems of banana, sugarcane and potato have been cultured in this way.
groundedIn: §10.1 — even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus; remove the meristem and grow it in vitro to obtain virus-free plants; banana, sugarcane, potato

stem: What is the major advantage of producing plants by micropropagation?
solution:
The major advantage of **micropropagation** is that a **large number of plants can be propagated in a very short duration**, and all of them are **genetically identical** to the original plant from which they were grown (they are **somaclones**).

Thus desirable varieties are multiplied true to type on a commercial scale; tomato, banana and apple have been produced this way. Combined with meristem culture, the method also yields virus-free plants.
groundedIn: §10.1 — propagation of a large number of plants in very short durations; producing thousands of plants through tissue culture is micro-propagation; each plant genetically identical to the original, i.e., somaclones; tomato, banana, apple on commercial scale; meristem culture gives virus-free plants

stem: Crystals of Bt toxin produced by some bacteria do not kill the bacteria themselves because –

options.label: A
options.text: bacteria are resistant to the toxin

options.label: D
options.text: bacteria encloses toxin in a special sac.

solution:
**(c) toxin is inactive.**

In Bacillus thuringiensis the Bt toxin protein exists as an **inactive protoxin** in the crystals. It becomes an active toxin only inside an insect, where the **alkaline pH of the gut** solubilises the crystals. The activated toxin binds to the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, causing swelling, lysis and death of the insect.
groundedIn: §10.1 — the Bt toxin protein exist as inactive protoxins; converted into an active form due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilise the crystals; activated toxin binds midgut epithelial cells and creates pores

stem: What are transgenic bacteria? Illustrate using any one example.
solution:
**Transgenic bacteria** are bacteria whose DNA has been manipulated (by recombinant DNA technology) so that they carry and **express a foreign gene**, i.e., genetically modified bacteria.

**Example: production of human insulin in E. coli.**

1. Human insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, **chain A and chain B**, linked by **disulphide bridges**.
2. In **1983, Eli Lilly**, an American company, prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin.
3. These sequences were introduced into **plasmids of E. coli**, and the transgenic E. coli produced the insulin chains.
4. Chains A and B were produced separately, extracted and combined by creating **disulphide bonds** to form human insulin.

Such **genetically engineered insulin** is structurally identical to natural human insulin and does not cause the allergic reactions that animal insulin (from slaughtered cattle and pigs) sometimes caused.
groundedIn: §10.1; §10.2.1; §10.3; Fig. 10.3 — organisms whose genes have been altered by manipulation are GMOs; animals with DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are transgenic; Eli Lilly 1983 introduced DNA sequences for A and B chains into plasmids of E. coli; chains extracted and combined by disulphide bonds; animal insulin caused allergy; human insulin made in bacteria is identical to the natural molecule (stated in the chapter Summary)

stem: Compare and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of production of genetically modified crops.
solution:
GM crops offer large gains in yield, stress tolerance and nutrition, but they carry ecological, health and socio-economic risks.

| Basis | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| Stress tolerance | Crops made more tolerant to **abiotic stresses** (cold, drought, salt, heat) | Genetic modification can have **unpredictable results** when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem |
| Pesticide use | **Reduced reliance on chemical pesticides** (pest-resistant crops such as **Bt cotton**) | The transgene may spread to wild relatives, and the toxin may harm non-target organisms |
| Yield and losses | Reduced **post-harvest losses**; higher crop yields | Pests may develop resistance to the toxin over time |
| Soil | **Increased efficiency of mineral usage**, preventing early exhaustion of soil fertility | Long-term effects on soil organisms are not fully known |
| Nutrition and health | **Enhanced nutritional value**, e.g., **golden rice** (Vitamin 'A' enriched rice) | Foreign proteins in GM food may cause **allergic reactions** in some people |
| Industry and economy | Tailor-made plants supply starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals to industries | **Patents** on GM varieties and **biopiracy** of traditional varieties (e.g., Basmati) harm farmers |

Because of these risks, GM crops are regulated; in India **GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee)** decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services.
groundedIn: §10.1; §10.4 — GM crops tolerant to abiotic stresses, reduced reliance on chemical pesticides, reduced post harvest losses, increased efficiency of mineral usage, enhanced nutritional value (golden rice), tailor-made plants for starches, fuels, pharmaceuticals; unpredictable results when introduced into the ecosystem; GEAC; patents, Basmati, biopiracy; BEYOND CHAPTER: spread of the transgene to wild relatives, harm to non-target organisms, pests developing resistance to the toxin, unknown long-term effects on soil organisms, allergic reactions to GM food

stem: What are Cry proteins? Name an organism that produce it. How has man exploited this protein to his benefit?
solution:
**Cry proteins** are the insecticidal **Bt toxin** proteins coded by the **cry genes**. They form protein crystals and kill certain insects such as lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).

**Organism:** the bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis** (Bt).

**Exploitation by man:**

1. Specific Bt toxin (cry) genes were isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis and incorporated into crop plants such as **cotton**, producing **Bt cotton**.
2. The genes are chosen according to the crop and the target pest, since most Bt toxins are insect-group specific: the proteins of **cryIAc** and **cryIIAb** control **cotton bollworms**, and that of **cryIAb** controls **corn borer**.
3. The toxin is made as an inactive protoxin; in the insect's alkaline gut it becomes active, binds the midgut epithelial cells, creates pores and kills the insect.
4. Such plants resist insects **without the need for insecticides**, in effect a **bio-pesticide**. Other examples are Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato and soyabean.
groundedIn: §10.1; Fig. 10.1 — Bt toxin produced by Bacillus thuringiensis kills lepidopterans, coleopterans, dipterans; toxin coded by gene named cry; cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, cryIAb controls corn borer; genes incorporated into cotton; resistance to insects without insecticides, a bio-pesticide; Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato, soyabean

stem: What is gene therapy? Illustrate using the example of adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
solution:
**Gene therapy** is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child/embryo. Genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease: a **normal gene** is delivered into the individual or embryo to take over the function of, and compensate for, the **non-functional gene**.

**Example: ADA deficiency**

1. **Adenosine deaminase (ADA)** is an enzyme crucial for the functioning of the **immune system**. Its deficiency is caused by **deletion of the gene** for ADA.
2. The **first clinical gene therapy** was given in **1990** to a **4-year old girl** with ADA deficiency.
3. Bone marrow transplantation or **enzyme replacement therapy** (functional ADA given by injection) can treat some patients, but neither is completely curative.
4. In gene therapy, **lymphocytes** from the patient's blood are grown in a culture outside the body.
5. A functional **ADA cDNA** is introduced into these lymphocytes using a **retroviral vector**, and the cells are returned to the patient.
6. As these cells are **not immortal**, the patient needs **periodic infusion** of such genetically engineered lymphocytes.
7. If the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at **early embryonic stages**, it could be a **permanent cure**.
groundedIn: §10.2.2 — gene therapy a collection of methods allowing correction of a gene defect; delivery of a normal gene to compensate for the non-functional gene; first clinical gene therapy 1990 to a 4-year old girl with ADA deficiency; ADA crucial for the immune system; deletion of the gene; bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy not completely curative; lymphocytes cultured, functional ADA cDNA introduced using a retroviral vector, returned to patient; periodic infusion; early embryonic stages could be a permanent cure

stem: Digrammatically represent the experimental steps in cloning and expressing an human gene (say the gene for growth hormone) into a bacterium like E. coli ?
solution:
The steps are drawn as a **flow chart** of boxes joined by downward arrows, in this order:

1. **Isolation of the gene:** mRNA for human growth hormone is isolated from human cells and copied into **cDNA** using **reverse transcriptase** (cDNA lacks introns, which E. coli cannot remove).
2. **Cutting:** the cDNA and a **plasmid vector** (with an origin of replication, a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene and a promoter) are cut with the **same restriction enzyme**, giving matching sticky ends.
3. **Ligation:** the gene is joined into the plasmid by **DNA ligase**, forming **recombinant DNA**.
4. **Transformation:** the recombinant plasmid is introduced into **competent E. coli** cells (e.g., treated with calcium chloride and given a heat shock).
5. **Selection:** transformed cells are picked out by growing them on a medium containing the antibiotic.
6. **Expression:** the transformed E. coli are multiplied in a culture (bioreactor) under optimal conditions, and they express the gene to make **human growth hormone**.
7. **Downstream processing:** the protein is extracted and **purified**.

Labels a marker looks for: human cell, mRNA, cDNA, plasmid, restriction enzyme, DNA ligase, recombinant plasmid, E. coli (host), selection, culture, purified hormone. The same route was used to make human insulin chains in plasmids of E. coli.
groundedIn: §10.0; §10.2.1 — creating optimal conditions for a catalyst to act; downstream processing technologies to purify the protein; DNA sequences for insulin chains introduced in plasmids of E. coli to produce the chains, which were then extracted; BEYOND CHAPTER: mRNA copied into cDNA by reverse transcriptase, introns not removed by E. coli, plasmid origin of replication, selectable marker and promoter, cutting with the same restriction enzyme to give sticky ends, joining by DNA ligase, competent cells made with calcium chloride and heat shock, selection on an antibiotic medium, culture in a bioreactor

stem: Can you suggest a method to remove oil (hydrocarbon) from seeds based on your understanding of rDNA technology and chemistry of oil?
solution:
Yes. Oil-free (or low-oil) seeds can be produced by **silencing the genes for the enzymes that make the oil**, using **RNA interference (RNAi)**.

1. **Chemistry of oil:** seed oil is a **triglyceride**, an ester of **glycerol** and **fatty acids**, made by enzymes of fatty acid synthesis and their assembly into triglycerides.
2. The gene coding for a key enzyme of this pathway is identified and isolated.
3. Using an **Agrobacterium vector**, a DNA construct is introduced into the plant so that it produces both **sense and anti-sense RNA** of that gene.
4. The two complementary RNAs form **double stranded RNA (dsRNA)**, which initiates RNAi and **silences the specific mRNA** of the enzyme, preventing its translation.
5. Without the enzyme, fatty acids or triglycerides are not synthesised, so the seeds of the transgenic plant **do not store oil**.

This is the same strategy by which RNAi silences the nematode mRNA in transgenic tobacco.
groundedIn: §10.1; Fig. 10.2 — RNAi involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA; using Agrobacterium vectors, genes introduced to produce both sense and anti-sense RNA forming dsRNA that silenced the specific mRNA; BEYOND CHAPTER: seed oil is a triglyceride, an ester of glycerol and fatty acids, made by enzymes of fatty acid synthesis

stem: Find out from internet what is golden rice.
solution:
**Golden rice** is a **genetically modified (GM) variety of rice** that is **enriched with Vitamin 'A'**. It is an example of genetic modification used to **enhance the nutritional value of food**.

Its grain contains **beta-carotene** (provitamin A), which gives it a golden-yellow colour. It is meant to reduce **vitamin A deficiency** in populations that depend on rice as their staple food.
groundedIn: §10.1 — genetic modification has enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g., golden rice, i.e., Vitamin 'A' enriched rice; BEYOND CHAPTER: the grain contains beta-carotene (provitamin A), giving its golden-yellow colour; meant to reduce vitamin A deficiency in rice-dependent populations

stem: Does our blood have proteases and nucleases?
solution:
**Yes.** Blood contains both proteases and nucleases, but their activity is **controlled**.

1. **Proteases** in blood include the enzymes of clotting such as **thrombin**. They circulate mostly as inactive precursors and act only when needed.
2. Blood also carries **protease inhibitors** such as **alpha-1-antitrypsin**, the human protein used to treat **emphysema**; they keep protease activity in check.
3. **Nucleases** (DNases and RNases) in plasma break down free DNA and RNA.

Because protease activity in blood is controlled, a protein drug such as **insulin** injected into the blood is not destroyed before it acts; it is the **digestive proteases of the gut** that make oral administration of such proteins difficult.
groundedIn: §10.2.1; §10.3 — insulin taken at regular intervals and the question whether insulin can be orally administered; human protein alpha-1-antitrypsin used to treat emphysema; BEYOND CHAPTER: blood contains proteases such as thrombin, circulating mostly as inactive precursors; alpha-1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor present in blood; plasma nucleases (DNases and RNases) break down free DNA and RNA; gut digestive proteases make oral protein drugs difficult
